laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os/-O3 with -G0; the fixture suite covers the laws it asserts, not every rule in the handbook

laws.title: Bitfields are allocated LSB-first in a container the size of the declared type and never straddle a 32-bit boundary; reads are narrowed and sign-extended, writes are masked read-modify-writes

source_anchor.note: Bitfield layout is decided by stor-layout.c plus the backend's bitfield access patterns; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: a 64-bit mask is built for a bitfield write
four bitfields totalling 32 bits take one word
40 bits cannot fit one word, so a second word is used

symptom: a field read uses lh or lbu instead of lw
a write contains li with a negative value followed by and/or
lever: bitfields fill their container from the least significant bit upward and never straddle a 32-bit boundary, so {unsigned a:20; unsigned b:20;} is 8 bytes with b in the second word

a read is narrowed to the smallest aligned access: a 16-bit field on a 16-bit boundary is a bare lhu, an unsigned field otherwise is lw plus srl plus andi, and a signed field is a sign-extending load (lh/lbu) plus sra
a write is a masked read-modify-write: li with a 64-bit negative mask, and/or, then sw - the mask immediate is the giveaway
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine. Layout and sizes: struct{unsigned a:1;b:3;c:12;d:16;} is 4 bytes with the fields at bits 0, 1, 4 and 16; struct{int a:1;b:3;c:12;d:16;} is also 4; struct{unsigned char a:3;b:5;} is 1 byte; struct{unsigned short a:4;b:12;} is 2; and struct{unsigned a:20;b:20;} is 8, with the second field starting in the second word rather than straddling. Reads: an unsigned 3-bit field at bit 1 is lw + srl 1 + andi 0x7; an unsigned 16-bit field at bit 16 is a bare lhu $2,2($4); a signed 12-bit field at bit 4 is lh $2,0($4) + sra 4; a 5-bit field in an unsigned char container is lbu + srl 3. Writes: p->c = v becomes lw, li $15,-65536 (a 64-bit mask), andi $5,$5,0xfff, ori $15,$15,0xf, and, sll $5,$5,4, or, sw.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that every bitfield read is a masked lw (aligned fields use a narrower load) and that a write is a shift-and-insert
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, synthetic structures with 1- to 20-bit fields in char, short and int containers; packed attributes and bitfields wider than their container were not measured

laws.title: Tail calls are jumps: -foptimize-sibling-calls is on at -O2/-Os/-O3, so a call in tail position becomes j target and the function may contain no jal at all - at -O1 it stays jal plus j $31

source_anchor.note: Sibling-call expansion happens in calls.c plus the backend's sibcall patterns; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: at -O1 a tail call is still jal plus j $31
at -O2 the same call is a bare jump

symptom: the target has no jal where your reconstruction calls a function
your reconstruction has jal plus j $31 where the target jumps straight out
lever: at -O2/-Os/-O3 a call in tail position is j target, so a function can end in a jump to an external symbol with no jal and no jr $31 at all
at -O0/-O1 sibling calls are not optimised: the same source keeps jal target plus j $31 - and 542 files in this project are built at -O1
the flag is the switch: -O1 -foptimize-sibling-calls turns the jumps on and -O2 -fno-optimize-sibling-calls turns them off
laws.receipt: At -G0 on this machine. int t1(int a){return g(a);} compiles to j g at -O2 and -Os, and to jal g followed by j $31 at -O0 and -O1. Adding -foptimize-sibling-calls to -O1 produces j g, and adding -fno-optimize-sibling-calls to -O2 restores jal plus j $31, so the transformation is exactly that flag and it is not enabled below -O2. The same jump appears in every tail position tested: with a local variable (int x=a+1; return g(x)), in both branches of an if/else returning from different calls, for a void call, and for return g(*p).
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a function's calls all appear as jal, and that the level does not change call shape
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O0/-O1/-O2/-Os with -G0 plus the two sibling-call flags, synthetic one-call functions

laws.title: volatile is visible as unmerged accesses: the same address is loaded once without it and once per mention with it, and a store stops being sunk into the return jump's delay slot

source_anchor.note: Volatility is honoured throughout the RTL passes rather than at one site; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the two non-volatile read-modify-writes merged
the volatile form keeps both

symptom: the target loads the same address twice where your reconstruction loads it once
the target stores to a pointer before the final j $31 where your build puts the store in its delay slot
lever: without volatile the compiler merges repeated accesses: *p = *p + 1 twice becomes one lw, addu ...,2 and one sw; with volatile each mention is its own lw/addu/sw
without volatile a store can be sunk into the delay slot of the following j $31; with volatile the sw stays before the jump
two loads from the same address in the target therefore mean the source read it twice through a volatile pointer, or that a call sits between the reads
laws.receipt: At -O2 and -Os on this machine, with the same shapes at both levels. void f(int *p){*p = *p + 1; *p = *p + 1;} becomes one lw, addu $15,$15,2 and one sw, while the volatile version becomes two lw/addu $15,$15,1/sw triples. int g(void){int a=*p; int b=*p; return a+b;} loads once without volatile and twice with it. For a global, gi = gi + 1 emits lw, addu 1, j $31, sw (the store is in the jump's delay slot) while the volatile version emits lw, addu 1, sw, j $31.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that repeated reads are always separate instructions (the compiler merges them) and that volatile only reorders accesses rather than changing how many there are
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 and -Os with -G0, synthetic functions reading and writing the same address twice; atomic builtins and volatile bitfields were not measured

laws.title: An aggregate copy is unrolled into lw/sw pairs up to 32 bytes and becomes an inline ldl/ldr-sdl/sdr loop above that - memcpy is never called

source_anchor.note: Aggregate copies go through store/load expansion (movstr patterns) in expr.c plus the backend; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: eight words are unrolled; nine words become a loop
ldl/ldr-sdl/sdr move 16 bytes per trip

symptom: the target has an ldl/ldr-sdl/sdr loop where your reconstruction calls memcpy
the target has a run of lw/sw pairs where your reconstruction calls memcpy for a small structure
lever: a copy of 32 bytes or less is fully unrolled into lw/sw pairs, one pair per word
a copy of more than 32 bytes becomes an inline loop moving 16 bytes per iteration with the unaligned ldl/ldr and sdl/sdr pairs - not a memcpy call, at any size tested up to 256 bytes
do not confuse ld/sd (aligned 64-bit, used for long and double) with ldl/ldr/sdl/sdr (unaligned, used by these copy loops)
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine, with void f(struct S *d, struct S *s){*d = *s;} for structures of 4 to 256 bytes. Copies of 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 and 32 bytes are unrolled into lw/sw pairs (2 instructions per word plus the return). At 36 bytes and above the compiler emits an inline loop: ldl/ldr pairs to load 16 bytes, sdl/sdr to store them, addiu to advance both pointers and a bne to close the loop - 14 to 20 instructions regardless of total size. No memcpy or memmove relocation appears at any size tested.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a large structure assignment becomes a memcpy call, and that copies use the aligned ld/sd pairs
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, structures of 4 to 256 bytes made of int fields; structs with padding, arrays of structs and memcpy with a known constant size were not measured separately

laws.title: An indirect call is jalr $reg with the target in an ordinary register, and it is never turned into a tail jump - even in tail position it keeps the call plus j $31

source_anchor.note: The indirect-call pattern is in the MIPS backend; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: indirect calls; the assembly prints jal $31,$reg
the same instruction as the compiler writes it

symptom: the target calls through a register where your reconstruction calls a named function
the target has jalr plus j $31 where the direct equivalent would be a bare jump
lever: an indirect call is jalr $reg (the assembly writes jal $31,$reg) with the target in an allocation-dependent general register - not $25 or $t9, so do not look for a fixed register

sibling-call optimisation applies only to direct calls: a function pointer called in tail position still saves $31, calls, restores $31 and returns with j $31, while the direct equivalent becomes a bare j target (L-EE-036)
the same shape appears at -O1, -O2 and -Os, so an indirect call tells you nothing about the level
laws.receipt: At -O2, -Os and -O1 with -G0, all three levels identical. int c1(int a){return gfp(a);} loads the global function pointer (lw $2,%lo(gfp)($15)) and calls jalr $2; a call through a structure field loads it from the struct, a function-pointer parameter is moved into $2 first, and a void pointer call uses jalr $4 - so the register is whatever the allocator picks. The object disassembles the instruction as jalr while the assembly writes it as jal $31,$2. In tail position the contrast with a direct call is complete: int d(int a){return g(a);} becomes a bare j g with no jal, while int i(int a){return gp(a);} keeps lw, jal $31,$2, ld $31 and j $31.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that an indirect tail call becomes a jump like a direct one (sibling calls only cover direct calls), and that an indirect call target travels in $25/t9
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os with -G0, synthetic function-pointer calls through a global, a struct field and a parameter; calls through arrays of pointers and varargs callees were not measured

laws.title: Comparisons used as values are materialised (== is xor plus sltu, <= is an inverted slt plus xori) and comparisons used as conditions either branch or become a branchless select with movn/movz; && is branchless and || is not

source_anchor.note: These are the backend's comparison and conditional-move patterns; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: equality is materialised as less-than-one
<= is an inverted, operand-swapped <

symptom: you expect beq/bne for == or != and find xor plus sltu
your reconstruction branches where the target has movz, or the reverse
lever: a comparison whose result is used as a value is materialised: a==b is xor $r,$a,$b plus sltu $r,$r,1, a!=b is the same xor plus sltu $r,$0,$r, a==0 is sltu $r,$a,1 and a<b is slt (sltu when unsigned)
a<=b is not one instruction: it is sltu/slt with the operands swapped (b<a) and then xori $r,$r,0x1
a comparison used as a condition branches on the operands instead (bne/beq), so a bare bne in the target means the source compared in an if/while
the two logical operators are not symmetric: a&&b is branchless (sltu plus movz) while a||b uses branches, and min/max use movz rather than branches
when both arms of an if are cheap values the compiler selects branchlessly with movn/movz, so movn/movz does not by itself mean the source used a ternary
laws.receipt: At -O2 and -Os on this machine, identical row for row. Materialised results: a==b gives xor $4,$4,$5 then sltu $4,$4,1; a!=b gives the same xor then sltu $4,$0,$4; a==0 gives sltu $4,$4,1; a!=0 gives sltu $4,$0,$4; !a gives sltu $4,$4,1; a<b gives slt (sltu unsigned); a>b gives slt with the operands swapped; a<=b gives slt $5,$5,$4 then xori $5,$5,0x1; a&&b gives sltu $5,$0,$5 then movz $5,$0,$4; a||b is branchy (bne, beq, li $2,1); a<b?a:b gives slt plus movz. As a condition the same comparison branches instead: if(a==b) emits bne $4,$5,$L with no xor or sltu, and a loop test if(i==3) emits xori $13,$12,0x3 with movz. The condition half has two outcomes, not one: with a call in one arm (if (a==b) return g();) the compiler branches (bne $4,$5,$L), but when both arms are simple values (if (a==b) return 1; return 2;) it converts the if into a branchless select - xor $4,$4,$5 then movn $2,$15,$4 - so a materialised xor paired with movn/movz can also come from an if statement. Which conditional move is picked is not fixed: -O2 uses movn with the constants in one order and -O1 uses movz with them swapped, so assert on movn-or-movz rather than on one of them.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that == compiles to beq, that <= is a single comparison instruction, and that && and || compile the same way
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 and -Os with -G0, synthetic one-expression functions over int, unsigned and zero comparisons; 64-bit comparisons and comparisons of floating-point values were not measured

laws.title: A 128-bit vector type compiles to lq/sq, is passed in a register pair, cannot be returned by value, and is the way to tell a 16-byte vector copy from a struct copy

source_anchor.note: The lq/sq patterns are EE-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: a 128-bit container is loaded with the MMI instruction
...and stored with sq

symptom: the target moves 16 bytes with lq/sq where your reconstruction uses lw/sw pairs
you are reconstructing a 16-byte value as a vector and the compiler rejects the return
lever: a mode(V4SI)/s128 value is loaded and stored with lq and sq, so lq/sq in the target means the source used a 128-bit type there, not a plain structure
the discriminator: the same 16 bytes copied as a struct unrolls into lw/sw pairs, copied as a vector becomes one lq plus one sq
a 128-bit parameter travels in a register pair from $4, its first element is extracted with dsll/dsra and later elements need the whole value spilled with sq and reloaded with lw

a 128-bit value cannot be returned by value - the compiler errors with 'output_operand: invalid expression as operand' - so a target function returning 16 bytes by value is a struct with a hidden pointer, never a vector
vector arithmetic is not supported in 3.2 (a + b on two vectors is an error), so these types are opaque 128-bit containers
laws.receipt: At -O2 and -Os with -G0, identical. With typedef int v4si __attribute__((mode(V4SI))): v4si x = *p loads with lq $2,0($4); *p = v stores with sq $5,0($4); *d = *s copies with one lq and one sq; ((int*)p)[i] is sll/addu/lw and the store form is sll/addu/sw; element 0 is extracted with dsll $4,$4,32 then dsra $4,$4,32 while elements 1 and 3 require sq $4,0($sp) followed by lw $2,4($sp) or lw $2,12($sp). A 16-byte struct copy of the same size is lw/sw pairs instead, so lq/sq is the discriminator. Returning a v4si by value fails to compile with 'output_operand: invalid expression as operand', and adding two v4si values fails with 'invalid operands to binary +'. In this project 1141 of the reconstructed source files use mode(V4SI) types.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that a 16-byte copy always unrolls into lw/sw pairs (a vector type uses lq/sq), and that a 128-bit value can be returned by value like a structure
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 and -Os with -G0, synthetic mode(V4SI) functions for load, store, copy, element access and parameter passing; the ABI slots beyond the first pair and unaligned lq/sq were not measured

laws.title: float lives in COP1 and double lives in general registers: l.s/s.s and c.lt.s plus bc1t against ld/sd plus dpadd and dpcmp, with no l.d anywhere

source_anchor.note: Which mode uses COP1 is decided by the port's patterns; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: single precision uses COP1
double precision uses libgcc
float comparisons branch in COP1

symptom: you cannot tell whether a target value is float or double
you are looking for l.d or c.lt.d in a target that does double arithmetic
lever: float lives in the COP1 registers: l.s/s.s to load and store, add.s/mul.s to compute, c.lt.s plus bc1t to compare, mtc1/cvt.s.w and cvt.w.s/mfc1 to convert
double lives in general registers: ld/sd move it, dpadd/dpsub/dpmul/dpdiv compute it, dpcmp compares it against an integer compare, and litodp/dptoli/fptodp/dptofp convert it
l.s/s.s/c.*.s/bc1t in the target means float; ld/sd into a GPR followed by jal dp* means double; there is no l.d or c.lt.d in this build at all
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine, with float and double globals and one operation per function. A float global is loaded with l.s $f0,%lo(gf)($15) and stored with s.s $f12,%lo(gf)($15); a double global is loaded with ld $2,%lo(gd)($15) and stored with sd $4,%lo(gd)($15), i.e. into general registers. float a+b is add.s $f0,$f12,$f13 while double a+b is jal dpadd; a float comparison is c.lt.s $f12,$f13 followed by bc1t while a double comparison is jal dpcmp followed by an integer compare and movn/movz. Conversions follow the same split: int to float is mtc1 plus cvt.s.w, float to int is cvt.w.s plus mfc1, int to double is jal litodp, double to float is jal dptofp, float to double is jal fptodp. Comparing against zero uses mtc1 $0,$f0 plus c.eq.s for float and dpcmp for double. The relocations in the object name dpadd, dpcmp (twice), dptofp, fptodp and litodp - and no l.d or c.lt.d appears anywhere.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that double uses the COP1 registers like float, and that a double comparison is a c.lt.d instruction
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, synthetic single-operation functions over float and double globals; arrays of floats, struct members and varargs were not measured separately

laws.title: 64-bit integer add, subtract, shift, bitwise and compare are native inline instructions (daddu, dsll, dsra, dsrl, slt); only multiply, divide and modulo call libgcc

source_anchor.note: The 64-bit GPR patterns are EE-specific (mainline MIPS would call libgcc); no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the R5900 adds 64-bit values inline
shifts are native, not libgcc calls
the narrow-a-64-bit-value-to-32-bits idiom

symptom: you expect a libgcc call for 64-bit arithmetic and the target has daddu or dsll
the target has dsll $r,$r,32 followed by dsra $r,$r,32
lever: 64-bit integer arithmetic is native: daddu/dsubu/daddiu for add, subtract and increment, dsll/dsra/dsrl for shifts, and/or/xor for bitwise, and slt for comparison
only multiply, divide and modulo leave the function: __muldi3, __divdi3, __moddi3, __udivdi3, __umoddi3 (L-EE-032)
int to long long is a no-op move because the ABI sign-extends a 32-bit argument; long long to int is dsll $r,$r,32 then dsra $r,$r,32, and unsigned to long long is dsll then dsrl
the dsll-32-then-dsra-32 pair is the 'narrow a 64-bit value to 32 bits' idiom and is also how element 0 of a128-bit vector is extracted (L-EE-041)
laws.receipt: At -O1, -O2 and -Os with -G0, identical, and the object contains no R_MIPS_26 relocation for this set. long long a+b is daddu $4,$4,$5; a-b is dsubu; a+1 is daddiu; -a is dsubu $4,$0,$4; a<<4 and a<<n are dsll; a>>4 is dsra (dsrl unsigned); &, | and ^ are and/or/xor; a<b is a single slt; a==b is xor plus sltu ...,1. A long long to int conversion is dsll $4,$4,32 then dsra $4,$4,32, an unsigned to long long conversion is dsll then dsrl, and an int to long long conversion is a bare move. Only multiply, divide and modulo are out of line, which L-EE-032 records as __muldi3, __divdi3, __moddi3, __udivdi3 and __umoddi3.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that 64-bit integer arithmetic is out of line like double arithmetic, and that a 64-bit compare needs a helper
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os with -G0, synthetic one-operation functions over long long and unsigned long long; 64-bit floating point and 128-bit values are covered by L-EE-029 and L-EE-041

laws.title: Unaligned access: a pointer cast emits a plain lw, a constant-size memcpy emits lwl/lwr or ldl/ldr pairs, and packed members emit ulw/usw - which are assembler pseudo-instructions

source_anchor.note: The unaligned patterns are EE-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: half of an unaligned word access
expands to lwr plus lwl, so the object never contains ulw

symptom: you see an lwl/lwr pair and cannot tell whether it is a copy or a packed member
you are grepping a disassembly for ulw or usw and cannot find them
lever: a pointer cast writes the plain instruction with the unaligned offset (lw $2,1($4)) - the compiler trusts the cast and synthesises nothing
a constant-size memcpy is expanded: 1 byte lbu/sb, 2 bytes lb/sb twice, 4 bytes an lwl/lwr pair stored with swl/swr, 8 bytes ldl/ldr stored with sdl/sdr

a packed structure member is written as the pseudo-instruction ulw/usw in the assembly, which the assembler expands into an lwr plus lwl (or swr plus swl) pair - so the object never contains ulw or usw and a packed access looks like any other unaligned word access
laws.receipt: At -O1, -O2 and -Os with -G0, identical. *(int*)(p+1) becomes lw $2,1($4) - a plain word load at an unaligned offset. memcpy(d,s,4) becomes lwl t4,3(a1), lwr t4,0(a1), swl t4,3(a0), swr t4,0(a0); the 8-byte form uses ldl/ldr and sdl/sdr; 2 bytes are lb twice plus sb twice; 1 byte is lbu plus sb. A member of a packed structure read as p->b is written ulw $2,1($4) in the assembly, and the object shows lwr v0,1(a0) followed by lwl v0,4(a0) - the pseudo-instruction expands to a pair, so grepping an object or a disassembly for ulw or usw finds nothing.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that an unaligned pointer cast is handled by the compiler (it emits a plain instruction), and that ulw/usw exist in the object
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os with -G0, synthetic functions using pointer casts, constant-size memcpy and a packed structure; unaligned double and 128-bit accesses were not measured

laws.title: Forward branches use the plain forms while loop back edges use the branch-likely forms (bnel, beql, bgtzl), whose delay slot runs only when the branch is taken

source_anchor.note: The branch-likely patterns are EE/MIPS-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the loop back edge is a branch-likely
beql against $0 is printed beqzl

symptom: a loop back edge is written bnel/beql/bgtzl instead of bne/beq, or the reverse
you are grepping for beql and only find beqzl
lever: the loop back edge uses the branch-likely form, so bnel/beql/bgtzl at the end of a body means a loop and its delay slot holds an instruction that must only run when the branch is taken
forward branches - if/else, guards, && and || - use the plain forms beq/bne/blez/bltz
the assembly writes beql/bnel while objdump prints beqzl/bnezl when the comparison is against $0, so grep for both spellings
at -Os an individual loop may be restructured into a plain branch plus an unconditional b back edge
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine: if (p == 0) return -1; uses a plain beq, if (x) return 1; uses beq/bne, if (a && b) uses beq/bne, and an if/else chain uses beq. Loops differ: while (n--) ends in bnel, for (i=0;i<n;i++) has a blez guard and a bnel back edge, do { } while (n > 0) ends in bgtzl, and while (*p == 0) p++ ends in beql. The likely form's delay slot runs only when the branch is taken, which is why a bnel at the bottom of a loop can carry the loop's own work (at -O1 the same loop puts its mult in that slot). -O1 and -O2 agree; at -Os the while (*p == 0) p++ loop is restructured to a bne plus an unconditional b. The assembly spells these beql/bnel while objdump prints beqzl/bnezl against $0. A 170-file sample of this project's matched sources shows bnezl 11 times and beqzl 7 times, alongside addiu 384, move 322, ld 267, sd 235 and jal 185.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a loop back edge uses the same branch form as an if, and that beql always appears as beql in a disassembly
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os with -G0, synthetic loop and branch shapes plus a 170-file instruction-mix sample of the project's matched sources; branch prediction annotations were not measured

laws.title: Every move is daddu $d,$s,$0 - a 64-bit copy - and objdump prints it as move, so the mnemonic never reveals the encoding

source_anchor.note: Which move pattern the backend picks is port-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured from the object encodings.

constants.means: every move is DADDU, the 64-bit form
ADDU, the 32-bit form, is never used for a copy

symptom: your reconstruction writes addu $d,$s,$0 and the bytes do not match
you are grepping a disassembly for daddu and the histogram shows none of them
lever: the compiler copies registers with the 64-bit form, so every move in the object is daddu $d,$s,$0 (funct 0x2d) - even when the C type is int
objdump prints daddu $d,$s,$0 as move, which is why a mnemonic histogram of real code shows move but no daddu at all
addu (funct 0x21) is never emitted as a copy, so writing addu $d,$s,$0 in a reconstruction will not match the bytes
in practice most moves are argument shuffling (targets a0/a1/a2), a large minority fill branch and jump delay slots, and move $d,$0 materialises zero
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine, decoding the object words of int c32(int a){int b=a;return b;} and long long c64(long long a){long long b=a;return b;} gives 0x0080102d for both - DADDU v0,a0,zero, the 64-bit special-function code 0x2d, not ADDU's 0x21. The same holds for every move in the sample: int x=0 and long long x=0 both produce 0x0000102d, and g(b,a) produces 0x0080782d, 0x00a0202d and 0x01e0282d. Because objdump renders daddu $d,$s,$0 as move, a 170-file mnemonic histogram of this project's sources lists move 322 times and daddu zero times. A 60-file context count of 125 moves shows 48 in branch or jump delay slots, 57 in ordinary positions, 19 as move $d,$0, and targets dominated by a0 (46), a1 (18) and a2 (7).
laws.falsifies: the assumption that move expands to addu, and that the mnemonic tells you whether a copy is 32-bit or 64-bit
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, object-word decoding of synthetic 32-bit and 64-bit copies plus a 60-file context sample; moves of floating-point and vector values were not measured

laws.title: The printed mnemonic is an alias: li is ADDIU or ORI or a lui+ori pair, nop is sll $0,$0,0, beqz/bnez/b are beq/bne against $0, and move is daddu - so compare encodings, not spellings

source_anchor.note: The pseudo-instruction set is the assembler's, not the compiler's; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the table is measured by decoding object words.

constants.means: ADDIU, printed as addiu or as li for a small immediate
ORI, printed as li for an immediate up to 0xffff

symptom: your assembly says li and the target has addiu, or the reverse
two instruction streams look identical as text but differ in bytes
lever: li is a pseudo-instruction: an immediate within signed 16 bits becomes ADDIU, up to 0xffff becomes ORI (zero-extending), and anything larger becomes a lui plus ori pair which objdump prints as two instructions
nop is SLL $0,$0,0; beqz/bnez/b are BEQ/BNE against $0; move is DADDU $d,$s,$0 (L-EE-046); ulw/usw are LWR+LWL and SWR+SWL pairs (L-EE-044)

in a 60-file sample of this project's sources every encoding maps to one or more mnemonics but no mnemonic maps to two base encodings, so comparing encodings is always safe while comparing mnemonics is not
laws.receipt: Decoding object words at -O2 -G0. return 5 is ADDIU $2,$0,5 and return -5 is ADDIU $2,$0,0xfffb, both printed li; return 0xffff is ORI $2,$0,0xffff (also printed li); return 0x12345 is printed as lui v0,0x1 plus ori v0,v0,0x2345, two real instructions with no li alias. Over 60 files of this project's matched sources the encoding op=0x09 is printed addiu 110 times and li 35 times, SPECIAL funct 0x00 is printed nop 23 times and sll 3 times, op=0x04 is printed beqz 7 times and b twice, and op=0x05 is printed bnez 3 times and bne once - while no mnemonic in the sample maps to two different base encodings.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a mnemonic identifies an encoding, and that li is a real instruction
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, object-word decoding of synthetic immediates plus a 60-file mnemonic-to-encoding census; floating-point and vector pseudo-instructions are covered by L-EE-019, L-EE-041 and L-EE-044

laws.title: COP2/VU0 instructions cannot be produced from C by this compiler: vector types use lq/sq in general registers, vector arithmetic and by-value returns fail to compile, and only inline assembly emits lqc2/sqc2

source_anchor.note: The backend carries VU0 operand predicates and a -mvu0-use- flag, so the patterns exist; no C construct was found that reaches them, and the negative results are measured.

constants.means: the flag restricts which VU0 registers may be used
only inline assembly emits COP2 loads

symptom: the target contains lqc2, sqc2, qmtc2, qmfc2, cfc2, ctc2 or v* instructions and your C reconstruction cannot produce them
you are trying to express a VU0 operation with a vector type
lever: this compiler never emits COP2 from C: mode(V4SI) and mode(V4SF) loads, stores and copies use lq/sq in general registers, adding two vectors is a compile error, and returning one by value is a compile error too
the backend does carry VU0 machinery (vu0_register_operand and friends, plus the -mvu0-use-REG1-REG2 flag) but no builtin reaches it, and the v constraint is 'impossible' for a vector value
the one working path is inline assembly: asm volatile("lqc2 $vf1,0(%0)" :: "r"(p)) compiles and emits lqc2, so any COP2 instruction in a binary came from hand-written assembly in the original source
consequence for reconstruction: such sites cannot be matched by C alone - write inline assembly there, or accept that the function cannot be reproduced in C
laws.receipt: Measured on this machine at -O2 -G0. mode(V4SI) and mode(V4SF) loads, stores and copies compile to lq/sq in general registers, never to lqc2/sqc2; a + b on two vectors fails with 'invalid operands to binary +'; returning a vector by value fails with 'output_operand: invalid expression as operand' (V4SI) or 'unrecognizable insn' (V4SF); and using the v constraint on a vector value fails with 'impossible register constraint in asm'. The compiler does have VU0 support: --target-help lists -mvu0-use-REG1-REG2 and cc1 exports vu0_register_operand, vu0_dest_operand, vu0_field_operand, vu0_float_operand, vu0_int_register_operand, vu0_reg_imm5_operand and mips_vu0_use_range. Inline assembly works: asm volatile("lqc2 $vf1,0(%0)" :: "r"(&v)) emits lqc2, and the same with sqc2 emits sqc2.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a 128-bit or float-vector C type makes the compiler use the VU0, and that COP2 instructions in a binary could come from ordinary C
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0 with mode(V4SI) and mode(V4SF) types and inline assembly; the -mvu0-use- flag and the VU0 operand predicates are recorded but not exercised, and no attempt was made to reach COP2 through them

laws.title: Variable shifts are sllv/srav/srlv and integer negation is negu (two more alias pairs), float copy/negate/compare are mov.s/neg.s/c.le.s plus bc1t, and the second multiplier mult1 appears at -O2/-O3 but not at -O1/-Os

source_anchor.note: The operator patterns and the two multiplier units are backend- and EE-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the assembly writes sll $d,$s,$t
the assembly writes subu $d,$0,$s
the scheduler uses the EE's second integer multiply unit

symptom: the target has sllv, srlv or negu where your reconstruction expects sll, srl or subu
the target uses mult1 and you cannot produce it from C
lever: a shift by a variable amount is a register shift: the assembly writes sll/sra/srl $d,$s,$t but the object contains sllv/srav/srlv, so these are ordinary C expressions and not inline assembly

integer negation is nego in the object (the assembly writes subu $d,$0,$s); float copy is mov.s, float negation is neg.s, and float comparisons are c.lt.s/c.le.s/c.eq.s followed by bc1t (bc1f for the inverted test)

mult and mult1 are the EE's two integer multiplier units: at -O2 and -O3 the scheduler moves one multiply to mult1 when two can overlap (three independent multiplies, or a dependent chain), while -O1 and -Os use mult throughout - so mult1 in a target is a scheduling signal and also a level hint
madd.s was an open question in this entry and is resolved by L-EE-050: it comes from a sum of two or more products in one float expression
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine. a<<n gives sllv a0,a0,a1 in the object (sll $4,$4,$5 in the assembly), a>>n gives srav or srlv, and -a gives negu a0,a0 (subu $4,$0,$4); float negation is neg.s $f0,$f12, a float copy is mov.s, and a<=b is c.le.s $f12,$f13 followed by bc1t, with c.lt.s and c.eq.s for the other comparisons. The second multiplier: one multiply uses mult only; two independent multiplies still use mult only; three independent multiplies produce mult plus mult1; a dependent pair (x=a*b; return x*b;) also produces mult plus mult1; and the second multiplier is level-dependent (see below). No C spelling tried for a*b+c produced madd.s - it always compiled to mul.s plus add.s; L-EE-050 resolved this: a sum of two or more products in one expression uses the COP1 accumulator (mula.s plus madd.s), so madd.s is ordinary C after all. The second multiplier is level-dependent: the same three-multiply fixture compiles to mult three times at -O1 and -Os, but to mult twice plus mult1 once at -O2 and -O3. The earlier count that suggested -O2 and -Os agreed came from a different fixture (two independent multiplies), which uses mult only at every level. multu is not used for a plain unsigned 32-bit multiply (that is mult) - it appears when a 32-bit unsigned multiply must produce a 64-bit result, and the 64-bit forms also carry object suffixes dsrav (variable shift) alongside dsllv and dsrlv.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that sllv/srlv/negu in a binary indicate hand-written assembly, and that mult1 needs inline assembly
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2/-Os with -G0, synthetic one-operator functions over int, unsigned and float; other EE multiply-unit shapes and madd.s were not resolved

laws.title: A float expression that sums two or more products uses the COP1 accumulator (mula.s then madd.s, madda.s mid-chain, msub.s for subtraction) while a statement form does not, and float stores are swc1

source_anchor.note: The accumulator patterns are backend-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the first product goes into the COP1 accumulator
each further product is added in the accumulator
stores use the COP1 form, printed s.s in the assembly

symptom: the target has mula.s/madd.s (or madda.s/msub.s) where your reconstruction produces mul.s plus add.s
you cannot produce the madd.s you saw in the target
lever: a single float expression that sums two or more products is evaluated in the COP1 accumulator: the first product is mula.s, each further one madd.s, and a chain that needs the intermediate value uses madda.s; subtraction uses msub.s
a statement form (s = a*b; s += c;) or a loop accumulation uses mul.s plus add.s instead, so the accumulator is a signal that the source wrote the sum of products as one expression
the accumulator is hard register 71 (FP_ACC of L-EE-016), i.e. it is genuinely used
float stores are swc1 (printed s.s in the assembly) against lwc1 for loads - both are COP1 forms
the 64-bit shifts and negation appear in the object with a suffix: dsra32, dsrl32, dsllv, dsrlv and dnegu
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine. a*b+c gives mul.s plus add.s, but a*b+c*d gives mula.s $f12,$f13 followed by madd.s $f0,$f14,$f15; a*b+c*d+e*g gives mula.s, madda.s, madd.s; a*b+c*d+e gives mula.s, madd.s, add.s; and a*b-c*d gives mula.s plus msub.s. The statement form float s=a*b; s+=c; and the loop form for(...) s += p[i]*q[i]; both give mul.s plus add.s, so the accumulator depends on the expression shape rather than the operation. A float global store is swc1 $f12,off (s.s in the assembly) where the load is lwc1. In the object the 64-bit forms carry suffixes: dsra32, dsrl32, dsllv, dsrlv and dnegu, while the assembly writes dsra/dsrl by 32, dsll/dsrl by register, and dsubu $d,$0,$s. The accumulator also covers subtraction: an expression that subtracts products (c - a*b - d*e) compiles to mul.s plus suba.s plus msub.s (and msuba.s in other shapes), so the accumulator family is mula.s/madd.s/madda.s for sums and mul.s/suba.s/msub.s/msuba.s for differences.
laws.falsifies: the earlier note that madd.s could not be produced from C, and the assumption that a float multiply-accumulate always uses the accumulator
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 with -G0, synthetic float expressions over one to three products plus statement and loop forms; the same shapes for double go to libgcc (L-EE-029)

laws.title: A zero comparison in control flow becomes an inverted REGIMM branch (bltz/bgez/bgtz/blez with likely forms on the back edge), a negated float condition is bc1f, and sqrtf is inlined as sqrt.s

source_anchor.note: The branch patterns and the sqrtf pattern are backend-specific; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: a while (n > 0) loop exits on a blez test
the source wrote !(comparison)
sqrtf is recognised by name and becomes a COP1 instruction

symptom: the target branches with bltz/bgez/bgtz/blez where your reconstruction has no branch
the target uses bc1f and your reconstruction does not negate the condition
the target has sqrt.s instead of a call
lever: a comparison against zero becomes a REGIMM branch only in control-flow position; as a value it is materialised (L-EE-040) and a simple if with constant arms becomes branchless

loop conditions are emitted inverted as the exit test and that is level-independent: while (n > 0) produces blez and while (n >= 0) produces bltz at -O1, -O2 and -Os alike; the back edge itself is level-dependent - bgtzl/bgezl at -O2/-O3 but a plain b at -O1/-Os
on floats the source's condition is used as written for bc1t, so bc1f means the source negated the condition (if (!(a < b))), and bc1tl/bc1fl are the likely forms
sqrtf is recognised by name and inlined as sqrt.s rather than calling libm
laws.receipt: At -O2 -G0 on this machine. return a<0 and if (a<0) return 1; return 0; produce no branch at all (the first is materialised with slti, the second is converted to a branchless select), but while (n > 0) { s += n; n--; } emits blez as the exit test at -O1, -O2 and -Os alike (level-independent), while the back edge differs by level: at -O2 it is bgtzl with the loop's own addu in its delay slot, and at -Os it is a plain b with the loop restructured; while (n >= 0) emits bltz. On floats, if (a >= b) emits c.le.s with the operands swapped plus bc1t, while if (!(a < b)) emits bc1f, and a < 0.0f ? -a : a emits c.lt.s plus bc1tl plus neg.s. An extern float sqrtf(float) called with one argument compiles to sqrt.s $f0,$f12 with no call. The inlined math names are exactly sqrtf and fabsf in this compiler: sqrtf becomes sqrt.s and fabsf becomes abs.s, while every other libm name tested (sinf, cosf, floorf, copysignf, fminf and others) becomes an ordinary tail call (j sinf). The likely branch spellings include bltzl, blezl and bc1fl alongside bgtzl/bgezl/bc1tl.
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a zero comparison always materialises or always branches the same way, and that sqrtf is a libm call
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0, synthetic comparison, loop and float-condition functions plus sqrtf; other libm names were not tested for inlining

laws.title: No latency nops: COP1 loads, moves and compares are never padded, so floating-point instruction order is entirely scheduler-driven

source_anchor.note: Latency modelling lives in the port's scheduling description; no line was read from the shipped tree, so the absence is measured rather than read.

constants.means: a COP1 load is followed by its use with no padding
the move sits in a delay slot rather than after a nop

symptom: you are looking for a missing nop between a floating-point load and its use
an FP sequence's order differs from the target and you are attributing it to latency
lever: this compiler never inserts a latency nop: l.s is immediately followed by its use, cvt.w.s follows the load it consumes, and mfc1/mtc1 are placed in branch delay slots

therefore floating-point instruction order is decided by optimisation and scheduling alone - never by latency padding - so an order difference must be explained by a source-shape lever, not by a missing nop
the same measurement shows the scheduler reordering independent COP1 loads (a dot product loads offsets 0, 4, 12, 8 at -O2), and -O2 and -Os differing in FP loop order
laws.receipt: At -O1, -O2 and -Os with -G0. float f(float*p,float*q){return *p+*q;} is l.s $f0,0($4); l.s $f1,0($5); j $31; add.s $f0,$f0,$f1 - the add sits in the branch delay slot. int f(float*p){return (int)*p;} is l.s $f0,0($4) immediately followed by cvt.w.s $f1,$f0, then j $31 with mfc1 $2,$f1. float f(float*p){return *p;} puts l.s in the delay slot of j $31. A float comparison is l.s followed directly by mtc1/c.lt.s. Counting nops over five floating-point shapes (including a loop accumulation and a 64-bit double load) at all three levels gives zero in every case. The same compiles show the four loads of p[0]*p[1]+p[2]*p[3] reordered to offsets 0, 4, 12, 8, and the FP accumulation loop ordered differently at -O2 (mtc1 $0,$f1) than at -Os (mtc1 $0,$f0 plus mov.s $f1,$f0).
laws.falsifies: the expectation that a load-delay or COP1-latency nop should appear between a floating-point load and its first use
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O1/-O2/-Os with -G0, five floating-point shapes plus a double load; integer load delays and the 2.96 compiler were not measured here

laws.title: A copy records a hard-register preference on whichever side is a global pseudo

source_anchor.note: mainline gcc-3.2.3 set_preference (the shipped binary resolves set_preference to global.c:1967). T2, not T1: the shipped body was located and its effects observed, but its two branches were not read line by line in the disassembly.

symptom: a value prefers the register used on the other side of a copy, in the direction you did not expect
a preference appears that no source-level copy seems to justify
lever: do not replay the preference: record the mask before and after the call and read the bits that changed
reg_renumber already maps locally placed values to hard registers, so the recorded preference can point at a register that never appears in the source
laws.receipt: func_001d4b88 at -Os -fno-thread-jumps: 842 decoded set_preference calls, 84 changed a preference mask. Examples (effect-diff): allocno 2 +{5} (dest pseudo 151 -> src $a1); allocno 24 +{13,14} (the preferences point at $t5/$t6, the hard registers of the *destination* side, and are recorded on the source allocno); allocno 13/11 +{15} ($t7). The return-point diff agrees with the prune-entry snapshot.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that a preference only comes from a parameter's ABI home or from a same-direction copy
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -Os -fno-thread-jumps on one reconstruction (func_001d4b88); the rule text is mainline gcc-3.2.3 global.c

laws.title: Preferences are pruned before ordering: conflicts, fixed, caller-saved for call-crossing values, and out-of-class registers are removed

source_anchor.note: mainline gcc-3.2.3 prune_preferences (the shipped binary resolves it to global.c:1236). T2, not T1: the shipped body was located and its effects observed, but not read line by line.

symptom: a caller-saved preference visible in an expand dump is gone by the time ordering runs
a value that crosses a call keeps no preference at all
lever: check whether the preference survives pruning before blaming the choice rule
for a call-crossing value, shorten the live range or move the copy; a respelled copy cannot keep a caller-saved preference across the call
laws.receipt: func_001d4b88 at -Os -fno-thread-jumps: 83 allocnos changed a preference mask at expand, 112 at prune. Of the 6 allocnos that got no register, 4 carried only caller-saved preferences ({5} / {13,14} / {15}, calls_crossed 2-30) and left prune with empty sets; the other 2 (allocnos 12 and 9) had no preference at all. The greg dump prints its `;; N preferences:` lines after prune.
laws.falsifies: the reading that the preference list printed in a dump is the list the choice rule sees
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -Os -fno-thread-jumps on one reconstruction (func_001d4b88); the rule text is mainline gcc-3.2.3 global.c
